"Some manufactures ask stupid questions such as "how much heat can this frame take before permanent damage to the structural integrity of the chassis?" or "how do we make the invasive code properly avoid the countermeasures of a witch class mech?". Well fuck them because we ask the real questions, like "how many guns can we put on one guy?" and "how heavy of a tungsten ball can we shoot at high enough velocity to kill 10 men in a row?". Then we take those answers, turn them into cannons, slap em' on a prototype and BAM! good to GO. Fuck you Harrison eat shit this is real science."

- recovered log from fired IPS-N R&D worker

The Fitzgerald is not named for some daring brigand, terror of the high seas, or fearless rebel fighting against impossible odds. It is named after a tragedy, because for the longest time, that's all the Fitzgerald ever was. Originally a casualty of corporate reorganization and mismanagement, it bounced between team after team, each one being disbanded for one reason or another. Eventually, it was relegated to the lowest tier of development. Being sent to work on it was almost synonymous for being fired. And yet, after decades of rotting away as IPS-N's reject pile, the unthinkable happened. It was complete. To this day it stands as a testament to hard work, persevering and toiling away at thankless labor for the slightest chance at glory. Those who choose to pilot the Fitzgerald embody this, because it doesn't matter how many times you've been knocked down, how often you get turned into a heap of slag, or exploded into shrapnel. What matters is that you have a cannon nearly as big as you are, and there is nowhere for them to hide.

One of the earliest prototypes for mechanized combat the M/K2 heralds from a time before the integration of ammo feeds and every weapon needed to be manually reloaded. Because of this, the frame was entirely focused around trying to get around this major limitation through jury-rigged hybridized reloads or just straight up swapping to a new gun. This approach was ultimately a failure, however, as there was simply no way to deal with the high temperatures and the fragility of the O.R.S replenishment system. GMS scrapped the project entirely to focus on more reliable alternatives as was befitting their brand. The M/K2 was later rediscovered by janitorial staff during an archival purge and was spread on the Omninet among enthusiasts. Some brave pilots even choose to take updated versions into battle, trying to make use of its unique abilities with a modern arsenal.

Originally meant to quickly patch hull breaches, the Grit Latch Magnets are a uniquely ISP-N innovation. Consisting of a fine metal grit packed tightly into a sphere, upon activation the grit explodes outwards into a cloud, where it magnetically attaches to all nearby metal. Tiny thermal charges bound to the granules then quickly burn, melting it into a slag almost instantaneously. The result is an effective, if temporary, layer of armature.

The Barbarossa has offers a simple choice: you kill it and get swarmed by its friends, or you don't kill it and you get the business end of a ship-class spool weapon. With the start of the broadcasts, Harrison Armory decided to take this principle to the next level; why even let them have the choice? The Subutai is the next step, armed with the experimental diversion rail, it locks down the battlefield leaving a trail of destruction in its wake. Now sure, you can't annihilate a bunker from a ridge over, but it's the price you pay for unparalleled defensive artillery. At the end of the day, you are still a solid block of metal, and ain't nothing gonna stand in your way.

Horus pattern groups have always been a contentious subject, the lines between one group and another can be blurry and heated debates about them are a common sight on the omninet. Originally, the Myconid was thought to be an offshoot of the Balor, its form comprised of thousands of tiny nanites shifting and rippling like water. However, after the official designation of greenwash, the Myconid began to be more clearly differentiated due to its more benevolent properties. Unlike other types of nanites, greenwash is incapable of tearing apart material and can not replicate itself, working only to surround and protect its designated targets. These less aggressive properties have led many to misunderstand the Myconid, thinking it a kindness compared to its siblings. They could not be more wrong. It is myriad, a shambling mound of churning wash, an angel emitting halos of shimmering nanite spores, a machine of propagation and rot. To those who endanger the network, it is nightmare made material.

The Mourning Cloak was a triumph of design, a masterpiece of ideas folded and sculpted together into a perfect gestalt. But even perfection can be improved at Smith-Shimano. Every piece can be broken down and improved, each moving part can become its own triumph. And when these parts are put together, you can get something even stranger and more beautiful than before. Or you could get the Maidens Blush, a bastardized, overly designed, paracausal patchwork of ideas. This is of course not to say that it is not an effective frame, or even a bad one, merely that it stands against the typical design philosophies of SSC. It reached licensing to push the boundaries of what SSC can make possible. It does not build upon the Firmament-manipulation groundwork laid by its predecessor, it eschewed years of work to rely upon strange technology. All to prove that even the strangest ideas can be made manifest. It stands as a reminder that there is no such thing as more perfect, it is all just different facets of the same idea, and one day, that SSC will see the whole for what it truly may be.

The earth was made to be shattered, metal was made to be heated and broken and battered. The world was made to be destroyed piece by piece. The Vauban stands as the Harrison's testament to dominion, each piece bent towards the singular point of progress and control. With the vast amount of data being spewed out of the Broadcasts it was only a matter of time until something truly devastating was unleashed that really ought to have stayed unknown. The Vauban was built upon that something. Gravity control is a tough nut to crack, and even now its secrets are not yet all teased out of its potential, but HA found enough to work with, and work with it they did. By leveraging hyper localized gravity pulses, the Vauban can sunder the ground, turning it into a mass of dangerous shards that can rend and drag down unwary opponents. No one can beat gravity forever.

The Primrose is the flagship model of SSC's LIM-AMOK line, and the culmination of SSC's experimentations with Broadcast tech. Built to be a close range combatant, with significant evasive and diversion options, it excels with elegant melee combat while offering variable engagement distance options. It marks SSC's first foray into large scale hand-to-hand options with rapid limb extension and magnetic attachment points allowing massive weapons to be hefted around with ease. Its ability to quickly close the distance, control a wide area around it, and evade any retaliation, has made it a popular option for many pilots who prefer direct and efficient solutions, immaculately done.

Originally meant to act as Harrison Armory's primary skirmisher unit, the Leoleth was archived late into testing due to a critical issue that led to continual interference when pilots tried to use ranged targeting systems. Due to this bug and a lack of supporting technology, the Leoleth project was scrapped and its resources were cannibalized to be used elsewhere. With the start of the Broadcasts, HA realized the opportunity revive previously retired projects and the Leoleth was the most promising candidate. While its hydraulic systems still had significant compatibility issues with targeting, new breakthroughs in perpetual momentum transference gave the mech alternative impact rate adjustments. Upon its release the Leoleth quickly became popular for its ability to turn potential energy into rapid kinetic movement at unprecedented speeds. The Boolean nature of its rerouting systems allow the Leoleth to swap between being hypermobile and a force of nature in a matter of mere seconds making it exceptionally useful for variable engagement zones and complex environments.
